name: readFile() (promises)
desc: Reads the whole file and resolves to a Buffer, or to a string when an encoding is given. Rejects with a coded error such as ENOENT when the read fails.
body:
The import path matters: `node:fs/promises` gives the promise API directly, while `require('fs').promises` reaches the same functions through a property.

The whole file is loaded, so the memory cost is the file size plus a copy when an encoding is used. For a file above a few tens of megabytes, use `createReadStream` and `pipeline` instead.

A UTF-8 file saved by Excel can start with a byte order mark. Strip it with `text.replace(/^\uFEFF/, '')` before `JSON.parse`.

name: readFileSync()
desc: Reads a whole file and returns it directly, blocking until the disk answers. Fine in a startup script, wrong inside a request handler.
body: Sync calls block the event loop, so every other request waits while the disk works. They are acceptable in scripts, tests and startup code, and a bad habit inside an Express handler.

name: readFile() (callback)
desc: The original error-first form. The callback receives (err, data) and is called once.
body: Wrap it with `util.promisify` when the surrounding code is async, or import from `node:fs/promises` and skip the wrapper entirely.

name: writeFile()
desc: Writes data to a file, creating it when missing and truncating it when present. Accepts a string or a Buffer.
body: The default flag is `w`: the old content is gone as soon as the call starts. For an output another process reads, write a temporary file in the same directory and `rename` it into place, so the target is never half written.

name: appendFile()
desc: Adds data at the end of a file and creates the file when it does not exist. The newline is the caller responsibility.
body: `appendFile` uses the `a` flag, which writes at the end even when other processes append at the same time. Without the trailing `\n` the log becomes one very long line and every line reader sees a single record.

name: mkdir()
desc: Creates a directory, and with recursive true creates every missing parent and does not fail when the directory already exists.
body: A write into a missing directory fails with `ENOENT`, and the message points at the file, not at the folder. Create the output directory before the first write of a script, not after the first failure.

name: readdir()
desc: Lists a directory. With withFileTypes the result contains Dirent objects that know whether an entry is a file or a folder.
body: The order is whatever the filesystem returns, so sort before printing. `withFileTypes` avoids a `stat` call per entry, which matters in a folder with thousands of files.

name: stat()
desc: Returns size in bytes, modification time as a Date, and type checks. Follows symbolic links; lstat does not.
body: `stat` fails with `ENOENT` for a missing path, so use it to test existence only when you accept that race: the file can disappear between the check and the read. Handling `ENOENT` on the read itself is more reliable.

name: rm()
desc: Removes a file or, with recursive true, a whole directory tree. force true ignores a missing target.
body: There is no undo and no trash folder. Build the path from a known root and print it in a log before a recursive delete. `force` hides `ENOENT`, not permission errors.

name: rename()
desc: Moves or renames a path in one atomic step when both paths are on the same filesystem. This is the safe way to publish a finished file.
body: A reader either sees the old file or the new one, never a partial write. Renaming across devices, for example from `/tmp` to a mounted volume, fails with `EXDEV` and needs a copy plus delete instead.

name: copyFile()
desc: Copies a file byte for byte. With the COPYFILE_EXCL constant it fails instead of overwriting an existing target.
body: Use `copyFile` for a file, not `readFile` plus `writeFile`: the built-in copy does not build the content in memory and lets the platform use its fastest path.

name: path.join()
desc: Joins path segments with the platform separator and normalizes the result. Relative segments stay relative.
body: Joining with `+ "/" +` produces doubled separators and breaks on Windows. `join` also collapses `..`, which is what you want for a path built from parts.

name: path.resolve()
desc: Builds an absolute path, starting from the rightmost absolute segment or from process.cwd().
body: Use `resolve` when the result must be absolute, for example before comparing paths or passing one to another process. It depends on where the process was started, so it is a poor choice for a file that sits beside the source; use `join` with `__dirname` or the module URL there.

name: createReadStream()
desc: Reads a file in chunks instead of loading it whole. Chunks are Buffers unless an encoding is set.
body: Chunk boundaries fall anywhere, so counting lines per chunk gives a wrong total for the last line. Use `readline.createInterface` when the unit is a line and `pipeline` when the data only needs to move.

name: pipeline()
desc: Connects streams, handles backpressure, forwards errors, and destroys every stage when one fails. Resolves when the destination is finished.
body: `pipe` forwards data but not errors, and leaves the other streams open after a failure. `pipeline` closes all of them, which is why a failed run does not hang the process. Pass an async generator function as a stage when a full `Transform` class is more code than the job needs.

name: new Transform()
desc: A stream stage that takes a chunk in and emits zero or more chunks out. The callback must be called exactly once.
body: Holding state between chunks is allowed, but the leftover must be flushed in `flush` or it is silently dropped. Forgetting to call the callback stalls the pipeline with no error, which looks like a hang rather than a bug.

name: readline.createInterface()
desc: Turns a readable stream into an async iterator of lines without loading the file into memory. Handles lines split across chunks.
body: `crlfDelay: Infinity` stops a Windows file from leaving `\r` at the end of every line. Breaking out of the loop closes the interface and destroys the stream, so no manual cleanup is needed.
